II. THE RELATIONSHIP OF THE PROPOSED ACTION TO LAND USE PLANS, POLICIES, AND CONTROLS FOR THE AFFECTED AREA
The Northeastern Illinois Area contains one of the largest and most complex urban concentrations in the world. In 1965 its six counties contained an estimated 6,689,000 persons living principally in 250 municipalities and governed by 1,200 independent bodies. The area is expected to grow to more than nine million people by 1990. To meet the demands of this growth and to insure "the welfare, health, prosperity, moral and general well-being of all the people of this (Illinois) State," the Illinois General Assembly, in 1957, established the Northeastern Illinois Planning Commission (NIPC).
The enabling statute authorized NIPC to "develop and adopt...a comprehensive plan, to amend such plan when future developments so require and to cooperate with various units of government in comprehensive planning for future growth and development." The specific process of preparing the Comprehensive Plan was initiated by NIPC in August, 1963. At that time, a series of eight studies, referred to as the Basic Research Project, were undertaken to gather the background information necessary in the preparation of a comprehensive area plan. The above studies analyzed existing conditions and estimated projected needs in the fields of: Population and Housing, Sewage Treatment, Housing Quality, Land Use, Commercial Structures, Capital Expenditure, Industrial Development, and Metropolitan Goals.
Although there was as yet no comprehensive plan for the six county area, there was an expressway and transit plan which took into account most of Cook and DuPage counties and parts of Will and Lake counties. This plan was prepared by the Chicago Area Transportation Study (CATS) on the basis of a forecast of land use employment and population in 1980.
